items.title: Rashied Ali and Henry Grimes interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 30, 2009
items.q: then even some of the main jazz clubs will hire like the really name avant garde players like Cecil Taylor or Ornette Coleman

ctx.x: Well back, like in the 70s, like the early part of the 70s, I don’t know too much about the Dixieland but probably all even Dixieland and avant garde now, but not now, not so much now, because the avant garde is really popular in Europe. And I mean you know we get like huge crowds in Europe with this stuff. And it’s festivals attracts a lot of people from all around. But actually it really got a hold there more or less more so than here. In fact, most of the European players that play jazz are into avant garde…

then even some of the main jazz clubs will hire like the really name avant garde players like Cecil Taylor or Ornette Coleman and sometimes I even get a shot at it too, because I’m sort of like an old-timer now. And so we get to play in a lot of the major clubs here now. But in the 70s it wasn’t about to be had, you know. We were hurting for places to play, we were hurting for recording companies to record us, so we were forced to start our own kind of venues. We went into like into loft situations in New York…
Was that something like with the October Revolution?
